episode_title: Business Exit Planning: Stop Waiting for the Perfect Market | Chris Lento, EM Capital

real_qa.q: What is the biggest mistake business owners make when timing their exit from a company or property sale?
real_qa.r: Trying to time the market much like the stock market can be very difficult. When a market is running and you're at your time of five years with returns at or above projections, people often wait too long. When that market cycle turns and debt and capital becomes scarce, you're with everyone else trying to exit. Sticking to your plan and taking singles and doubles as hits works better than waiting for a home run every time.

real_qa.q: How does EM Capital use downside-first underwriting to protect investors when market conditions turn negative?
real_qa.r: Downside-first underwriting means running scenarios asking what if rents are flat, what if rents go down, what if cap rates expand, or what if interest rates go up. Having longer-term debt gives more options to hold through a down cycle. The approach balances being realistic while making investors aware of downside possibilities and being conservative enough to provide protection. Preservation of capital is the number one rule.

real_qa.q: What specific value-add strategy does EM Capital use to increase net operating income on multifamily properties before exit?
real_qa.r: The primary way is through renovations and value-add by identifying properties with management problems, expense problems, market perception problems, or deferred maintenance. Interior renovations allow adding approximately $200 per month in rent per unit. Times 12 divided by the cap rate, this drives the price increase at sale. The ideal property has multiple issues like poor appearance, outdated interiors, and needed roof or parking lot work.

real_qa.q: When should business owners start planning their company exit according to real estate investment principles?
real_qa.r: You plan your exit when you buy. At underwriting, EM Capital projects the model out usually 10 years and factors in the best available debt, typically targeting a five-year hold. They project rent growth, value-add, and expense growth, locking these assumptions at purchase. Depending on how the property performs and market conditions, they reassess quarterly or every six months, and start prepping for sale about a year out by trimming expenses and driving occupancy.

real_qa.q: How does EM Capital structure deals to manage property operations remotely from Boston across the Southeast?
real_qa.r: EM Capital partners with mid-sized third-party property management companies managing 10,000 to 25,000 units, a sweet spot where they have systems and processes in place with multiple management layers, but EM Capital is not just a blip on their radar. Each deal uses multiple LLCs with separate bank accounts, separate management LLCs, separate partnership LLCs, and separate SEC syndication filings. They treat property managers as partners, develop relationships by visiting properties and dining with management teams, and have their contact information readily available.
